editorialSections.heading: Graphic, publisher and data source
paragraphs: The supplied infographic is Visual Capitalist’s “Ranked: The World’s 100 Biggest Pension Funds,” published 24 November 2022. Research/writing: Jenna Ross. Design: Sam Parker. The image credits Thinking Ahead Institute and Pensions & Investments (September 2022). The complete rank, fund, market and rounded-asset data are reconstructed below and checked against the publisher’s structured table.

The original legend uses circle size for total assets, a number for global rank and rings for ranks 1–100, with the largest funds on inner rings. Logos, country colors and flags identify entries; they are not investment-quality ratings. The table replaces the oversized visual while preserving its data and source record.

editorialSections.heading: Reporting cutoffs and source exceptions
paragraphs: The default cutoffs in the image are 30 September 2021 for US funds and 31 December 2021 for non-US funds. Exceptions dated 31 March 2022: Canada Pension, Pension Fund Association in Japan, BT Group in the UK and Organization for Workers in Japan.

The image marks estimates for National Social Security in China, Public Institute for Social Security in Kuwait, Boeing, Employees’ Provident in India, AT&T, General Motors, Employees’ Pension Fund in India, Ford, Wells Fargo, Verizon, J.P. Morgan Chase and Social Insurance Funds in Vietnam.

Other cutoffs: 1 January 2022 for Russia’s National Wealth Fund; 30 June 2021 for AustralianSuper, Aware Super, QSuper, UniSuper and Sunsuper; 31 March 2021 for Canada’s Public Service Pension Plan and the UK’s Universities Superannuation and Electricity Supply Pension; 31 January 2022 for Germany’s Bayerische Versorgungskammer.

The graphic predates the 2022 QSuper/Sunsuper merger and displays both separately. It says Royal Bank of Scotland Group and Lloyds Banking Group amounts are global group figures. These footnotes belong to the historical source, not a refreshed dataset.

editorialSections.heading: Country annotations retained from the graphic
paragraphs: Japan: the graphic describes GPIF as a defined-benefit plan for public-sector employees and says it had led the ranking since 2002. United States: it describes nearly half the top 100 as US funds, totaling more than $6 trillion. These are historical source descriptions, not independently updated findings.

India: the graphic describes Employees’ Provident contributions totaling 26.16% of earnings, split 13% employer, 12% employee and 1.16% government. This is preserved as a dated chart claim, not current contribution guidance.

China: the graphic describes National Social Security as a top-up fund financed through government, lottery ticket sales and state-owned enterprises, with a Yahoo Finance September 2020 attribution. Russia: it reports a $16 billion National Wealth Fund withdrawal to help cover the 2022 budget deficit, citing Reuters October 2022.

Norway: the chart says its Government Pension Fund held investments in more than 9,000 companies across 70 countries and was the largest single owner in world stock markets. UK: it describes the largest listed funds as company plans or industry pools. Both statements are retained as historical chart annotations.

Sweden: the graphic describes the AP funds as part of the national pension system for people who have worked and paid taxes in the country. Canada: it describes Healthcare of Ontario as a defined-benefit healthcare-workers’ plan based on employment earnings and years of contribution. These source summaries simplify scheme details and are not eligibility or benefit rules.

notes: The combined reference also includes 17 reviewed costing/investment expressions from the later study upload. Four analyst-signal expressions remain undefined and are identified as needing clarification. Repeated expressions can have different source contexts.
